title: From decision to settlement: how Korean immigrant parents raising a child with disabilities respond to disabling socio-educational environments
authors: Yoon H. Lee, Jisun Lee, Jinwoo Lee
abstract: This phenomenological study examines the lived experiences of six Korean mothers who immigrated to the United States to seek more inclusive educational opportunities and post-school supports for their children with disabilities. Grounded in disability studies, the analysis traces parents’ narratives across three stages: the decision to migrate, early settlement, and long-term adjustment. Findings reveal that migration was driven by structural barriers in Korea, concerns for children’s adulthood, and parents’ belief that more supportive systems existed abroad. After immigrating, parents became proactive advocates and navigated linguistic, cultural, and bureaucratic barriers while developing expertise within U.S. service systems. Over time, parents described greater satisfaction with educational and disability services while continuing to experience emotional strain, and redefined their quality of life, independence, and belonging. This study highlights how immigration becomes a prolonged journey where families emerge as active agents in resisting disabling environments and rebuilding possibilities for their children’s futures.

title: Disability type matters: structural discrimination in employment access and retention in Turkey
authors: Büşra Yüksel Güngör, Kemal Yavuz
abstract: Despite legal frameworks, quota obligations, employment incentives and active labour market programmes, the par­ticipation of people with disabilities in Turkey’s labour market remains limited. Turkey is a salient case because a developing-country labour market coexists with an extensive formal policy framework whose inclusive effects are constrained by weak enforcement, fragmented institutional coordination and persistent social prejudice. Based on semi-structured interviews with employees with disabilities, employers, İŞKUR officials, NGO representatives and parents of disabled individuals, this study examines structural barriers to employment access and retention. The findings show that discrimination varies by disability type. People with visible, severe, intellectual or psychosocial disabilities face stronger exclusion during recruitment, while those with invisible or milder disabilities are often preferred. Concerns about safety, productivity and workplace adaptation confine many disabled workers to low-skilled and low-visibility jobs. Policy gaps further undermine inclusion. The study argues for a contextual and interactional understanding of disability employment.

title: Ambiguities on disabled bodies in artworks: a Critical Iconology perspective
authors: Stella Christofi
abstract: This research situates itself at the intersection of disability studies and visual studies, employing a methodology informed by Critical Iconology as developed by Aby Warburg to analyze the representation of the disabled body in artworks in the twentieth century. It critiques and extends the discourse around the cultural perception of disability, by examining visual representations of impairment across diverse artworks between1920–1999. The study collects and maps images of the disabled body from different periods, examining the meanings of signs and patterns of impairment by adopting the critical theoretical frame of the social model of disability and ableism. Critical Iconology provides the tools to understand what the images say through cultural and social political circumstances. This research seeks to dismantle stereotypes and advance a nuanced understanding of the disabled body as depicted in visual arts.

title: Accessibility or misbehaviour: ableism in theatres
authors: Nicole Brown
abstract: Recent public debates about actors challenging audience members’ smartphone use during live theatre performances have foregrounded etiquette, distraction and theatrical immersion while overlooking smartphones’ role in enabling disabled people’s cultural participation. This article examines the tensions between normative expectations of audience behaviour and the use of smartphones as interfaces for accessibility technologies. Drawing on scholarship on ableism, psycho-emotional disablism and disability disclosure, it argues that framing smartphone use as inherently inappropriate reproduces exclusionary assumptions about legitimate participation. Disabled audience members risk having their access needs misrecognised, experiencing scrutiny and feeling compelled to disclose personal information to justify their behaviour. Such pressures can undermine belonging and discourage cultural participation. The article argues for an ethics of anticipatory access, in which theatres and cultural organisations develop policies that recognise diverse modes of participation without requiring disabled people to explain or defend their needs. It positions accessibility as a shared institutional responsibility rather than an individual accommodation.

title: Leading the pack: assistance dog team instruction from a universal design perspective
authors: Tiamat Warda
abstract: This article examines how disabled assistance dog professionals adapt traditional work practice norms to meet their needs and those of clients and assistance dogs. Based on nine interviews and 16 survey responses collected from disabled assistance dog professionals and their clients across Europe, this article identifies adaptations involving communication, session planning and structure, technology use, and, at times, the involvement of the professional’s assistance dog as their co-worker. Rather than solely compensating for disability, professionals frequently innovate more traditional practices that benefit the assistance dog team, offering potential new ways to approach instruction for the broader assistance dog sector to consider. The article speaks to a significant gap in literature concerning the work of assistance dog professionals with disabilities, and provides data to support a more accessible and inclusive assistance dog sector through universal design.

title: Families as subjects of need and knowledge: epistemic misrecognition in disability welfare policy in Norway
authors: Rosemarie van den Breemer
abstract: This article explores how Norwegian welfare policies aiming to ‘recognize families as resources’ align with the lived experiences of families caring for children with multiple disabilities. Drawing on qualitative data, the article examines parents’ experiences through a lens of professional family partnership and theories of epistemic injustice and social recognition. The article develops the notion of ‘epistemic misrecognition’ to describe three dimensions of feeling unacknowledged in these family accounts: families feel unheard in their testimony (testimonial misrecognition); they feel dismissed as relevant participants in inquiry (participatory misrecognition); and especially mothers experience misrecognition of their care-based expertise (misrecognition of experiential knowledge). These findings underscore both the importance of valuing families’ expertise in policy and practice and the barriers to doing so. While Norwegian next-of-kin policies recognise families as subjects of need, they are less able to acknowledge families as subjects of knowledge and fall short in granting families full epistemic standing.

title: Having choices and being supported: a co-research project about independence and Down syndrome
authors: Ashley Scott, Staci Christensen, Augusta Edouard, Benjamin Golden
abstract: Independence can look different for each person. People with Down syndrome are living longer, and many get support from professionals to grow their independence. We wanted to understand how health professionals support independence for people with Down syndrome. We used co-research method where team members with Down syndrome collaborate on all stages of the research process. Co-researchers interviewed 8 health professionals and 2 with Down syndrome about independence. We asked about communication, daily life skills, health, employment, and independent living. Using an inclusive process, we analyzed our data by coding transcripts, finding big ideas and patterns, then came up with themes. We found that health professionals mostly support independence for health, communication, and life skills. They want adults with Down syndrome to be independent, make choices, and get help from others when needed.

title: Co-production using Theory of Change in the development of the SUCCEED Africa community-based rehabilitation intervention for people living with psychosis in West and Southeast Africa
authors: Julian Eaton, Olubukola Christianah Omobowale, Rita Frinue Tamambang, Rachel Greenley
abstract: Psychosis and other severe mental health conditions cause substantial disability and reduced functioning across a number of domains. Services in low- and middle-income settings are often weak, and predominantly biomedical. Community-Based Rehabilitation (CBR) offers a comprehensive and person-centred approach that is aligned to effective case management models. The Support, Comprehensive Care and Empowerment for People with Psychosocial Disabilities (SUCCEED) programme was co-produced with people living with psychosis in four sub-Saharan countries, with a view to improving quality of life, mental health outcomes, and community participation. This paper described the intervention development process, using multiple iterations of Theory of Change (ToC), incorporating situation analysis, formative research and piloting. We present these iterations as results, using the GUIDED framework for intervention development, and the intervention is described using the TIDieR framework. We conclude that ToC can promote participatory processes of intervention co-development, as well as generate research questions. Interventions must remain flexible, and be open to revision, even if having core active ingredients.

title: Calling All Restroom Revolutionaries!
authors: Simone Chess, Alison Kafer, Jessi Quizar, Mattie Udora Richardson
abstract: Everyone needs to use bathrooms, but only some of us have to enter into complicated political and architectural negotiations in order to use them. The fact is, bathrooms are easier to access for some of us than for others, and the people who never think about where and how they can pee have a lot of control over how using restrooms feels for the rest of us. What do we need from bathrooms? What elements are necessary to make a bathroom functional for everyone? To make it safe? To make it a private and respectful space? Whose bodies are excluded from the typical restroom? More important, what kind of bodies are assumed in the design of these bathrooms? Who has the privilege (we call it pee-privilege) of never needing to think about these issues, of always knowing that any given bathroom will meet one’s needs? Everyone needs to use the bathroom. But not all of us can.

title: Integrating Disability, Transforming Feminist Theory
authors: Rosemarie Garland‐Thomson
abstract: My title here, “Integrating Disability, Transforming Feminist Theory,” invokes and links two notions, integration and transformation, both of which are fundamental to the feminist project and to the larger Civil Rights Movement that informed it. Integration suggests achieving parity by fully including that which has been excluded and subordinated. Transformation suggests re-imagining established knowledge and the order of things. By alluding to integration and transformation, I set my own modest project of integrating disability into feminist theory in the politicized context of the Civil Rights Movement in order to gesture toward the explicit relation that feminism supposes between intellectual work and a commitment to creating a more just, equitable, and integrated society.

title: The Academic Origins of Disability Studies and the Society for Disability Studies
authors: Rosemarie Garland‐Thomson, Rannveig Traustadóttir, Nirmala Erevelles
abstract: Based on a conversation with Rosemarie Garland-Thomson, this chapter examines the scholarly and academic labor involved in the emergence of critical disability studies in the United States, with particular attention to efforts to foreground disability culture, access, and justice across a wide range of institutions and communities. It explores how disability studies has critically interrogated cultural representations of disability and how, especially within the humanities, the field has reframed disability as a minority discourse rather than a medical problem. Through this shift, critical disability studies has challenged oppressive narratives and made visible more liberatory ways of understanding disability. Central to this account is the leadership and influence of Steve Taylor, whose vision and work were instrumental in shaping the field’s intellectual foundations and ethical commitments.

title: The Color of Violence
authors: Nirmala Erevelles
abstract: As I write this chapter, I am very conscious I am writing in a time of war. Almost daily there are reports of roadside bombs detonating; the launching of military offensives; power failures; and shortages of food, drinking water, and fuel in the “postwar” contexts of a devastated Afghanistan and an occupied Iraq. Not much has changed since President Obama announced the complete pull-out of U.S. troops from Iraq and Afghanistan in the near future. Here, in the United States, a few news media organizations keep diligent count of U.S. soldiers killed in the war. Even more infrequently, and almost always as a passing note, we hear a rare report of disabled war veterans returning from combat. While there are some reports of civilian deaths in Afghanistan and Iraq, I have been unable to find reports of Afghan and Iraqi civilians and members of the military (and now the insurgency) who have become disabled as a result of the war and the postwar conflict. I find this extremely troubling, but neither the alternative press nor radical scholars in the academy seem perturbed by these omissions.

title: Introduction
authors: Rannveig Traustadóttir, Nirmala Erevelles, Zana Marie Lutfiyya, Rachael A. Zubal-Ruggieri
abstract: In June 2023, a group of international scholars and former doctoral graduates of Syracuse University gathered for a reunion to reflect on their years as students and colleagues. As they shared memories of their intellectual journeys, one theme emerged with remarkable clarity and unanimity: the professor who had most profoundly shaped their thinking, their values, and their aspirations as scholars was Professor Steven J. Taylor. Many confessed that, throughout their careers, they had quietly measured themselves against the kind of academic Steve Taylor was – and they hoped to become. Steven J. Taylor (1949–2014) was a humble giant in disability studies. Reluctant to seek the limelight, he nonetheless exerted an immense and enduring influence on the field. His scholarship was instrumental in reconceptualizing disability as a socially constructed category of difference, challenging medicalized and deficit-based understandings that had long dominated research, policy, and practice. Yet Steve was never a detached academic. He believed deeply that research and scholarship must matter – that they must make a tangible difference in the lives of disabled people and contribute to social change, justice, and human dignity.

title: Belonging, Dignity, and Justice
authors: Rannveig Traustadóttir, Zana Marie Lutfiyya, Nirmala Erevelles
abstract: The book’s concluding chapter brings together personal and scholarly reflections on the legacy of Steven J. Taylor, offered by disability studies scholars and advocates who have not contributed to earlier sections of the book. These accounts situate Taylor’s influence within the international development of disability studies. The contributions reflect on the distinctive role of Syracuse University and the Center on Human Policy as an intellectual and moral home where disability studies was practiced, integrating scholarship, advocacy, and community life. Collectively, the reflections highlight how Taylor’s work reshaped understandings of disability as socially produced, relational, and fundamentally tied to questions of dignity, belonging, and human rights. Contributors emphasize Taylor’s enduring influence through mentorship, collaboration, and the formation of scholars and advocates across disciplines and national contexts, illustrating how his work generated ripples that continue to shape disability studies globally. The chapter concludes by identifying future directions for the field, including renewed attention to institutionalization and resistance to the contemporary backlash against disability rights. In doing so, it affirms that Steve Taylor’s legacy endures not only in texts and institutions, but also in the values and practices that continue to guide disability studies as a project of justice, inclusion, and collective responsibility.

title: Rethinking Community as Praxis
authors: Nirmala Erevelles, Susan Burch
abstract: Through a reflective conversation, we – Nirmala Erevelles and Susan Burch – as disability studies scholars draw on our different disciplinary backgrounds to identify connections to Steve Taylor and his work. Centering on Steve Taylor’s scholarship about intellectual disability, particularly through his concept of a sociology of acceptance, Erevelles theorizes disability in ranging contexts – historical, contemporary, American, and the Global South. Burch’s work on the history of deaf people and institutionalization identifies relationships and locations that overlap with, and move beyond, Steve Taylor’s research. An emphasis on relational analyses provides a launching-off point for further theorization and historicization. Pondering the implications of Taylor’s work on our field(s), we trace the ways our scholarship builds on, and at other times critiques, his work. Telescoping out, we identify arguments to meet some of the theoretical and methodological challenges that mark our field. Collectively marking the continuities and discontinuities from Steve Taylor’s scholarship and our own, we return to the beginning, reimagining community as a form of praxis.

title: The Influence of Steven J. Taylor on Disabled Lives and Disability Studies
authors: Rannveig Traustadóttir, Nirmala Erevelles, Zana Marie Lutfiyya, Rachael A. Zubal-Ruggieri
